opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting intersections right now, because these two worlds have historically been quite separate. On one side you have neural networks, which are incredibly flexible and powerful but fundamentally statistical, so we don't get guarantees. On the other side you have formal methods and theorem provers like Lean, where everything is rigorous and every step is checked, but writing those proofs by hand is extremely laborious.

What Lean offers is a common language where you can state properties precisely and have a trusted kernel check them. So if you want to say something about a neural network's robustness, for example that within some epsilon-ball around an input the output classification doesn't change, or that a network satisfies certain Lipschitz bounds, you can formalize that as a theorem. Then the question becomes: can we actually prove it, and can we prove it at scale?

That's where the two directions come together. One direction is using Lean to verify properties of neural networks. There's been work on verification tools based on bound propagation and SMT solvers, but those are often separate pieces of software that themselves could have bugs. Bringing that reasoning into Lean means the certificates can be checked by a small, trusted kernel. You get much stronger assurance that the verification itself is correct.

The other direction, which I find even more transformative, is using neural networks to help write those proofs. That's what we did with LeanDojo and related efforts: training language models to suggest tactics, retrieve relevant premises from the math library, and search for proofs. The beauty is that Lean gives you perfect feedback. The model can hallucinate all it wants, but the proof checker will tell you whether it's correct. So you get the creativity of the neural network, grounded by the rigor of formal verification.

When you combine those, you start to get this virtuous cycle: AI helping generate proofs about AI systems, with Lean as the arbiter of truth. Of course there are real challenges. Formalizing floating-point arithmetic is messy, networks are huge, and specifying what "robust" or "safe" even means for real-world tasks is hard. But I think this is the path toward trustworthy AI, especially in scientific and safety-critical domains, where we can't just rely on empirical benchmarks. We need guarantees, and Lean is giving us a practical way to get there.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because these two worlds have historically been quite far apart. On one side you have neural networks, which are incredibly powerful but essentially black boxes, and on the other you have formal methods, where every claim comes with a machine-checked proof. Lean is interesting to me because it's becoming the bridge.

The first piece is that Lean is a proof assistant, so if you want to make a statement like "this network's output stays within some bound when the input is perturbed within an epsilon ball," you can actually state that as a theorem and have the kernel check the proof. There's no hand-waving. That matters enormously when you're deploying these systems in safety-critical settings, whether that's control for a drone or a robot, or decision-making in a hospital. Empirical robustness, where you throw adversarial examples at a model and see what breaks, is useful, but it only tells you about the attacks you tried. A formal guarantee tells you about all of them within the specified region.

The second piece, and this is what's exciting right now, is that neural networks can help write those proofs. Historically, formal verification was bottlenecked by human effort. Writing proofs in Lean is slow and requires real expertise. But language models trained on Lean, with the proof checker acting as a verifier in the loop, can now propose proof steps, get feedback, and iterate. So you have this loop where the network generates candidate proofs and Lean plays the role of the ground-truth oracle. It's the same pattern we see with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, except the reward here is literal mathematical correctness, which is about as clean a signal as you can get.

So what that enables is verifying properties of neural networks using neural networks themselves as the proof-search engine, with Lean making sure nobody is cheating. And beyond robustness, I think this extends to verifying things like the correctness of a learned physics simulator against conservation laws, or showing that a controller respects a safety constraint. We have neural operators that can learn solutions to PDEs orders of magnitude faster than traditional solvers, but a domain scientist rightly asks, "how do I know this is right?" If you can attach a formal certificate to parts of that pipeline, that question starts to have a real answer.

The honest caveat is that we're still early. Scaling formal verification to the size of modern networks is hard, and much of the work involves abstraction, verifying properties of a simplified or bounded version of the system. But the direction is clear to me. Lean gives us a shared language where machine learning and formal reasoning can finally talk to each other, and the networks are getting good enough to speak it fluently.

astra-6.text:
I see Lean as a way to bridge the flexibility of neural networks with the rigor of formal verification. A neural network can perform well on a test set, but that alone doesn’t establish robustness. You want to specify a property—for example, that the predicted class stays the same under a bounded perturbation—and prove that it holds under clearly stated assumptions.

The neural network, or another AI system, can help propose a proof or find useful intermediate bounds. Lean then checks the mathematical argument. So the system generating the proof doesn’t have to be trusted; the proof has to pass the checker.

The challenge is scale. For large networks, those proofs can be very expensive, and the specification matters enormously. A guarantee about one class of perturbations doesn’t establish safety in every real-world setting. But this gives us a path toward precise, checkable guarantees that complement empirical testing.

sol-6.1.text:
I see Lean as a way to bridge the gap between finding evidence that a neural network is robust and actually proving a precise robustness property. Testing against adversarial examples is useful, but passing those tests doesn’t establish that there isn’t another perturbation that will cause a failure.

With a proof assistant, you can specify the property you care about—for example, that the predicted class stays the same within a defined neighborhood of an input—and check a proof of that statement. Neural networks could help propose bounds, intermediate lemmas, or proof strategies, while Lean checks whether those steps are valid.

The challenge is scale, and also making sure the specification captures what we actually mean by robustness. A guarantee under one perturbation model doesn’t automatically imply reliability in the real world. But this combination is exciting: learning can guide the search, and formal verification can provide a much stronger foundation for trusting the result.
